accuracy.evidence: Checked against the KS3 Physics programme of study (magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets), NGSS MS-PS2-3, IOP Spark pages on the field round a wire and on electromagnets, and the AQA KS3 syllabus 3.2. The wire's field direction follows the right-hand grip rule (current towards you gives an anticlockwise field; the needle code uses the tangent (sin, -cos) of the position angle and was checked at the right of the wire, where it points up). The coil field arrows leave the north end and enter the south end outside, and run south to north inside. The clip numbers are a stated model (clips in proportion to turns times current, iron x10, steel x8, copper x1, capped at 20); the adult text says strength rises with current and turns and that iron is magnetised by the coil, and items that use proportion say 'in a simple model'. Soft iron losing its magnetism and steel keeping some is standard KS3/GCSE content.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented KS3 misconceptions (IOP Spark, AQA teacher guidance): compasses point at the wire rather than round it (prediction and challenge 'radial'), a coil has no field at its ends (prediction), any metal core helps (copper core in the fair-test step and the 'copper' slip), changing two variables at once (the lab names both changed variables and refuses the conclusion; 'fair' slip), electromagnets switch off because the iron runs out (the 'core' slip), reversing the current changes the strength (the 'stronger'/'stop' slips) and a longer wire making it stronger (the 'length' slip).

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is built on this topic's own mechanisms: a compass whose needle angle is computed from the wire field plus Earth's field (so it points nearly north far away), a coil wound by dragging with a field that grows with turns and swaps ends on reversal, a fair-test bench that compares each test with the previous one variable by variable, a switch-off scene where soft iron drops all clips and steel keeps 40%, and a use sort. The gate measures it under 30% similar to every flagship lab, including flagmagfield and flagpoles, which cover permanent magnets.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each idea by doing: switching on swings the ring of compasses into a circle and reversing turns every one round; moving the compass away shows it drift back to north; tapping the wrong end of the coil says field lines go into it, so it is south; each fair test reports exactly what changed and the clip count change, and a two-change test is named and rejected; switching off a soft iron core drops every clip while steel keeps some. Playwright real-drag tests confirmed the probe, winding, magnet-lowering and sorting replies.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions with tempting wrong options the lab disproves: 'Straight at the wire' (the compasses line up round it), 'Nothing: the circles cancel out' for a coil (the field appears like a bar magnet's), 'Get weaker: iron blocks the field' (the iron core multiplies the clips), and 'They stay stuck' for soft iron when switched off (they all fall). The done message names what the learner predicted.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven rotating questions with answers in rotating positions; every wrong option has a slip tag with its own message: copper (not magnetic), length (more resistance, less current), core and battery (the field comes from the current), fair (two changes at once), radial and none (compasses line up round the wire; only far away do they point north), stronger and stop (reversal swaps poles, same strength), steel (stays magnetised so it cannot let go), fewer and same (more current, more clips).

readability.evidence: validate_lessons.py passes the readability limits (kid at most 6.5, adult at most 9.5). Kid paragraphs use short sentences and name one idea each ('Switch off the current and the field stops.'); key terms (field lines, turns, core, soft iron) are introduced in context. Canvas prompts fit a fixed two- or three-line strip, and the results table uses a monospace font so its columns line up.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one thing: field round a wire, coil like a bar magnet, three ways to make it stronger, switching off. Adult paragraphs give curriculum links and key words, the physics and the iron versus steel point, named mistakes, and what the lab does plus a battery safety note. The filler gate passes.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots and canvas dumps at iPhone 13 (390 px) in light and dark and at desktop for every step before and after Show me. Fixes made from them: the 'drag me down' hint overlapped the core buttons and then ran off the right edge (now left of the magnet with more space above it), use names overflowed the sort boxes (short names in the boxes), the Show me compass landed on a ring compass (probe spots moved outside the ring, button spots at 0.55 R), and the coil's inside field arrow was hidden under the turns (drawn on top). Canvas pills and steppers are 46-54 px tall.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin with a descriptive aria-label ('Move the compass above the wire', 'Wind one more turn on the coil', 'Say the right end is the north pole', 'Use soft iron as the core', 'Lower the magnet onto the clips and record the test', 'Fridge magnet holding a picture: a permanent magnet is fine'); the canvas aria-label is updated live with each reply; the challenge uses real buttons and a polite live region; axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in both themes on desktop and phone in the browser gate.
